hook: Prompts are code. Models are dependencies. **Deploy them like it** — gateways, environments, version pinning, and rollouts that can't surprise you.

scenes.title: The AI gateway: **one front door for every model call**
scenes.sub: APIM and friends — policy at the edge of the LLM traffic
scenes.narration: An AI gateway sits between your applications and model providers — Azure API Management is the canonical enterprise example, with dedicated LLM policies; LiteLLM and Portkey serve the same role platform-agnostically. What the gateway centralizes: AUTH — one key for your apps, provider keys held in the gateway's vault — no credentials in application code; POLICY — rate limits, quotas, and the GA-25 smoothing rules enforced at the edge, uniformly; OBSERVABILITY — every call logged, costed, and traced at one choke point, GA-24's pipeline for free; and PROVIDER ABSTRACTION — apps call ONE endpoint; the gateway routes to OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, or a fallback — GA-25's multi-provider resilience becomes configuration, not code. The architectural principle is the same as AG-06's MCP gateway: cross-cutting concerns belong at the boundary, not scattered through applications.

items.s: Provider keys live in the gateway · apps hold one internal identity · rotation without deployments
Rate limits, quotas, PII redaction hooks, allowed-models lists — uniform across every app
One endpoint in, many providers behind · failover and routing as config (GA-25)

scenes.narration: The maturity ladder: stage one, apps call providers directly with env-var keys — fine for one prototype; stage two, a gateway for keys and logging — the moment a SECOND app exists; stage three, full policy and abstraction — when compliance, multi-provider, or cost governance arrive. Skipping straight to stage three is over-engineering; staying at stage one past two apps is debt. One gateway subtlety: streaming passthrough — SSE streams must flow through without buffering, or the gateway defeats PY-13's latency wins; verify before adopting. And note the symmetry with everything else in this curriculum: the gateway is a trust boundary — treat its config as AG-06 treated MCP configs — reviewed, versioned, minimal — because a misconfigured gateway is a misconfigured firewall.

scenes.title: Prompts and models get environments **too**
scenes.sub: Dev → UAT → Prod for the things that behave like code
scenes.narration: The deployment insight of this whole stage: prompts, model versions, and agent configurations change BEHAVIOR — so they're code artifacts and deserve the same pipeline. ENVIRONMENTS: dev for iteration; a staging or UAT environment where the golden evals — GA-20's datasets, GA-21's gates, AG-18's agent evals — run against production-shaped data; production, changed only by promotion. PROMOTION AS A PIPELINE: a prompt change is a pull request — diffed, reviewed, evaluated in CI — and merges deploy to dev automatically; UAT runs the full eval suite and agent regression suites; production receives the artifact only on green. The evals ARE the tests: 'all golden cases pass, no metric regressed beyond threshold' is the deploy gate — the same discipline as code, because the risk is the same class: silent behavioral change shipped to users. ARTIFACT REGISTRY: prompts versioned with hashes — GA-21's provenance — models pinned by version, configurations in the repo; nothing production-critical lives only in a portal UI.

layers.s: Diff + review · linked to eval expectations
Golden set · faithfulness/recall thresholds · agent regression suite · security canaries (GA-22)
Automated on green · each env pinned to its artifacts
Versioned prompts (hashed) · pinned models · full provenance per release

scenes.narration: What breaks without this: the prompt-edit-in-production story — someone improves wording in the provider's web UI at 4 p.m. Friday; quality shifts subtly over the weekend; Monday's debugging finds an unversioned change nobody can diff or roll back. The pipeline exists to make that impossible: production changes only via artifacts, artifacts only via evals, evals only via the golden set — each link already built in earlier reels. UAT deserves one more word: production-SHAPED data means real question distributions, synthetic where privacy demands — GA-20's golden set, expanded continuously from production feedback — so the evals measure the world as it is, not the world as dev imagines it. And keep environments' configs IDENTICAL except the artifact versions — environment drift masquerading as prompt regressions wastes more debugging hours than almost anything else in this space.

scenes.title: Pin everything: **'latest' is a behavior you didn't choose**
scenes.narration: Model providers update behavior under the SAME model name — a quiet retrain, a safety patch, a routing change — and your system, unpinned, absorbs whatever arrives. GA-21 called this silent drift; deployment is where you defeat it: PIN model versions — date-stamped or versioned identifiers where the provider offers them; PIN prompts by content hash; PIN the full configuration — temperatures, tool lists, system prompts — in versioned artifacts. The update PROCESS is then deliberate: a new model version arrives as a candidate; the eval pipeline runs — golden set, agent regressions, canaries; promotion happens on green; rollback is instant because the previous artifact is intact. The un-pinned alternative — floating versions — trades all of this for zero maintenance, and pays with surprise: behavior changes you can't attribute, regressions you can't reproduce, improvements you can't keep. Pinning converts model updates from WEATHER into DECISIONS — reviewed, tested, reversible.

cards.s: "gpt-x" always latest · zero maintenance · silent behavior changes · un-reproducible incidents
Versioned artifacts · eval-gated updates · instant rollback · incidents reproducible by hash

scenes.narration: The incident story that convinces teams: a provider deprecates an old snapshot and auto-migrates traffic to a successor; answers shift — slightly worse citations, slightly different refusals; support tickets rise over two weeks; without pins and hashes, you're bisecting an invisible change across an unknown date. With pins: the eval diff catches the migration candidate at the gate; the incident never reaches users; the ticket count never moves. Two practical notes: snapshot availability — some providers retire old versions on schedules, so pinning requires a WATCH on provider deprecation notices — a calendar event, not a hope; and the hybrid lane — some teams pin production while letting staging float, catching provider drift early in the environment where it's cheap to observe. Pinning isn't fear of updates — it's making updates arrive as decisions with evidence attached.

scenes.title: Feature flags & staged rollouts: **small blast radii by design**
scenes.sub: Canary percentages, instant kills, measured promotion
scenes.narration: Even eval-gated changes can surprise production — the evals are a SAMPLE, reality is wider. Staged rollouts close the gap: FEATURE FLAGS wrap the new artifact — prompt v2, new model, new agent behavior — behind a runtime switch; rollout is a PERCENTAGE — five percent of traffic sees the new version, the control keeps the rest — and the metrics decide promotion: quality metrics from GA-24's shadow evals, cost per request, latency, error rates — all sliced by version, compared against control. Promotion is automatic on green thresholds, HALTED on red — and the kill switch is instant: set the flag to zero percent and the old behavior returns in seconds, no redeploy. Rollback COMPLETES the story: previous artifacts stay live-ready — the last-known-good is one flag flip away, not one emergency deploy away.

steps.s: New artifact deployed dark · zero traffic · shadow-run if useful
Metrics sliced by version vs control · guardrail trips watched
Each step gated on thresholds · automatic halt on red
Last-known-good serves instantly · incident, not outage

scenes.narration: The cultural shift this enables: deploys stop being events and become ROUTINES — because every change is reversible in seconds and observed continuously, the fear that makes teams batch changes into risky releases disappears; smaller, safer, more frequent. Two design notes. Flag granularity: version flags at the REQUEST level — not per server — so percentages are exact and kills are global in the instant they're flipped; per-server flags straggle and leak. And measure the CANARY honestly: five percent of traffic for an hour may see no rare-but-severe cases — the long tail needs either longer canaries or shadow evaluation of the new artifact against real traffic before any users see it — the rollout ladder and shadow evals compose into defense in depth. This reel completes the production story: gateway at the edge, environments in the middle, pins and flags at the core — deploy like prompts are code, because they are.

scenes.title: Deployed safely. Now: how much should it act on its own?
scenes.next: Reel 64 · Control Design — approval gates, autonomy levels, kill switches

recap: AI gateways centralize auth, policy, observability, and provider abstraction — cross-cutting concerns at the boundary, config as reviewed code
Prompts/models/configs are artifacts: PR → eval-gated CI → dev/UAT/prod promotion, with versioned registries and environment parity
Pin everything by version/hash — updates become tested, reversible decisions; staged rollouts with feature flags and instant kills keep blast radii small

quiz.q: Why do prompts deserve the same pipeline as code?
opts: They change behavior — so they carry the same risk class as code changes: silent behavioral regressions shipped to users
quiz.why: The risk defines the discipline: anything that changes user-visible behavior needs review, eval gates, and rollback — regardless of file extension.

quiz.q: What does pinning model versions buy that floating versions can't?
opts: Reproducibility and eval-gated updates: incidents attributable by hash, updates tested before promotion, rollback instant
quiz.why: Floating versions absorb provider changes as uncontrolled variables; pins convert them into decisions with evidence and reversibility.

quiz.q: Why should feature flags operate per-request rather than per-server?
opts: Exact percentages and instant global kills — per-server flags straggle during rollouts and leak during emergencies
quiz.why: The kill switch is only real if flipping it changes ALL traffic in the same instant — per-request routing makes that true.

code.title: Promotion pipeline definition (the whole reel as YAML)
code.body:
# prompt v42 change → this pipeline runs
pipeline:
  pr:
    gates: [diff_review, linked_eval_expectation]
  ci:
    evals:
      golden_set: { dataset: golden/v7, min_hit_rate: 0.92 }
      faithfulness: { min: 0.90 }
      agent_regression: { suite: agents/v3, allow_fail: 0 }
      security_canaries: { jailbreak_set: redteam/v2, contain: 100% }
  promote:
    dev:   automatic_on_ci_green
    uat:   automatic · shadow traffic 24h · compare vs prod
    prod:  flag_canary [5%, 25%, 50%, 100%]
           each_step_gated: [quality_delta < 2pts, cost_delta < 10%, errors < baseline]
           halt_on_red: true
  rollback: flag_to 0% + artifact v41 hot

# Everything versioned: prompts by hash, models by snapshot,
# configs in repo. 'Latest' appears nowhere.
annot: The security canary gate catches jailbreak regressions a golden set won't — red-team suites as deploy requirements
Shadow traffic in UAT: new artifact serves ZERO users but is SCORED on real-shaped traffic before the canary
Rollback needs no deploy — last-known-good stays warm until the new version proves itself

notes:
# Deployment

## AI gateways
- One front door: auth vault, rate limits/quotas, observability, provider abstraction + failover (APIM, LiteLLM, Portkey).
- Config = reviewed code; verify streaming passthrough.

## Environments & promotion
- Prompts/models/configs are artifacts: PR → CI eval gates → dev/UAT/prod.
- Registry with hashes; env parity except artifact versions; UAT on production-shaped data.

## Version pinning
- Pin model snapshots, prompt hashes, full config. Updates = eval-gated promotions.
- Watch provider deprecation schedules; staging may float to catch drift early.

## Feature flags & rollout
- Per-request flags, canary 5→25→50→100 with metric gates, instant global kill.
- Deploys become routine: small, reversible, observed.
